detail:

Tech stocks sank at the open on Wall Street - REUTERS/Jeenah Moon

Wall Street suffered its worst sell-off since Donald Trump's tariff rollout amid fears the Democrats will derail the AI boom.

The Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6pc on Thursday - the biggest fall since April 2025 - with shares in semiconductor makers the hardest hit.

The downturn was the worst since Mr Trump's so-called "liberation day", when he rolled out tariffs to countries around the world.

Investors fear the Democrats' midterm election victory will usher in tighter restrictions on AI companies, whose valuations have grown rapidly under Mr Trump.

Nvidia, which is the world's most valuable listed company, fell by more than 6pc while rivals including AMD and Micron plummeted 13pc and 11pc, respectively.

The companies make semiconductors that are used in data centres – huge buildings that power the models of AI companies.

Several Democrats which have won control of former Republican states have backed moratoriums on data centres in their local areas, potentially signalling a slowdown in demand for chips.

Elon Musk's empire also took a beating for a second day, with Tesla plunging 10pc and SpaceX falling 9pc.

The decline on Wall Street was in stark contrast to European markets. The FTSE 100 was 0.5pc higher, while the Cac 40 in Paris gained 0.7pc as investors switched out from AI stocks into more traditional industries.

Susannah Streeter, an analyst at Wealth Club, said: "A release valve has been unscrewed following the Democratic success of the midterms, with pent-up concerns about an escalation of the war in the Middle East evaporating.

"But sentiment around the AI trade remains fragile, with an expected slowdown in the data centre build-out still acting like a drag on the big tech sector players."

title: Elon Musk's SpaceX Default Risk Hits Record High as Democratic Sweep Adds to AI Rout
detail:
Elon Musk's SpaceX Default Risk Hits Record High as Democratic Sweep Adds to AI Rout
Daragh Thomas
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 1:00 PM PST 3 min read
SPCX
^NDX
^IXIC
Trade SPCX on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The cost of insuring SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) debt against default hit a record Thursday, as Democrats' election sweep raised political risks for Elon Musk's companies and an AI stock rout engulfed Wall Street.

SpaceX's five-year credit-default swaps widened as much as 14.6 basis points to 284.3 basis points.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has promised to freeze new data-center approvals, while Democratic control of Congress could bring greater scrutiny of Musk's businesses. SpaceX has explored several potential sites in the state, including building new facilities or converting warehouses, The Information reported in July.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote Wednesday.

The Nasdaq fell more than 10% below its October peak, entering correction territory. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slid as much as 10.2%, while the Nasdaq 100 faced an estimated $1.8 trillion wipeout, Reuters reported.

But default protection on major AI hyperscalers has become cheaper since the election, according to Bloomberg, even as SpaceX's costs have climbed.

Musk's AI Debt Warning Comes Home

Less than two weeks ago, Musk warned that debt markets had "almost entirely shut off access to money" for companies lacking substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

He predicted "guppy-level death and consolidation" among more than 200 specialist cloud providers.

Musk argued SpaceX was different, citing its investment-grade rating and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches. Yet his company's default insurance now costs more than ever.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) also saw its default insurance costs hit record levels Thursday, reflecting wider concerns about AI infrastructure financing.

SpaceX recently secured its GPU financing through a $40 billion lease commitment with Apollo Global Management Inc. (NYSE:APO), subject to closing conditions.

Its Super Intelligence division generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue but spent $16.44 billion on capital investments, more than twice the segment's revenue.

Tesla-SpaceX Merger Faces Political Test

The Democratic sweep has also raised questions about a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA).

The companies lost a combined $130 billion in market value Wednesday. Bloomberg reported that analysts had warned a Democratic victory could complicate a potential merger.

Kalshi traders still assigned roughly 71% odds to a binding merger agreement before 2028, down from 76% Monday. The probability of an agreement before May 2027 stood near 57%.

Credit: Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Key Takeaways

The Nasdaq 100 is down more than 10% since its most recent closing high in October, plunging into correction territory.

ETFs with top holdings in once-hot chip stocks are taking major hits on Thursday, while data center and AI infrastructure stocks have extended their declines.

The Blue Wave is throwing some cold water on the AI trade.

Today, a day after a post-election rally that followed a change of control in Congress, several once-hot corners of the tech sector are flagging—and buzzy AI ETFs that hold big helpings of AI-powered stocks are logging outsize declines—as investors try to determine the next phase of the tech trade.

For now, they aren't upbeat about it. Popular chip stocks took major hits, with SanDisk (SNDK), Western Digital (WDC), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Seagate Technology (STX) and Micron Technology (MU) among the biggest decliners in the S&P 500.

And AI infrastructure and data center stocks including Vertiv (VRT), Quanta Services (PWR) were down in the double digits, poised to notch losses for a second consecutive day. The Nasdaq 100 was recently off more than 10% from its most recent closing high in October, technically indicating correction territory.

The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM), which invests in memory stocks, was down about 15% on Thursday, veering closer to the price at which it started trading earlier this year than it has since the spring. Among longer-tenured ETFs including the iShares Semiconductor (SOXX) and WisdomTree AI and Innovation Fund (WTAI), the former is down about 10% today while the latter is close to wiping out its 2026 gains.

Roundhill's Neocloud ETF (NCLD), which launched in August, is now below where it started. And some leveraged long ETFs, which seek to multiply the daily moves of certain stocks or indexes, are getting hit too. The Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF (SOXL), which aims to triple the NYSE Semiconductor Index's daily return, has declined more than 30% today.

Summary List

Investing.com -- Wall Street suffered a broad selloff Thursday, with the Nasdaq 100 plunging as much as 6% and the S&P 500 falling as much as 3.8%, as an intensifying liquidation of artificial intelligence and data-center stocks raised fresh questions about the financing behind the industry's massive infrastructure spending boom.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

The market's biggest concern is becoming increasingly circular: AI stocks are being sold, weakening confidence in the industry's ability to raise capital, just as Anthropic prepares for what could become one of the largest initial public offerings in history. If the offering struggles, investors may become even more concerned about how the next phase of AI infrastructure spending will be financed.

The selling has also spread beyond technology, with investors increasingly choosing to reduce risk rather than rotate into other parts of the market.

AI infrastructure trade loses its buyers

The selling has been particularly severe among the companies supplying the infrastructure behind the AI boom, including semiconductor manufacturers, data-center operators, power providers and so-called neocloud companies.

During October's bouts of volatility, investors generally viewed weakness in the group as a buying opportunity, maintaining that robust demand for computing power would eventually overcome concerns about valuations, financing costs and construction delays.

That attitude appears to have changed significantly over the past two sessions. Investors who previously bought the dips are increasingly stepping aside, while others are liquidating positions amid mounting performance pressure and uncertainty over the industry's next phase.

The deterioration in sentiment accelerated Wednesday after Bloomberg reported growing concerns at Microsoft about the neocloud industry, which has attracted tens of billions of dollars in contracts to supply computing capacity to major technology companies.

Delays, regulatory obstacles and elevated costs have complicated the business models of these operators, many of which have borrowed heavily and committed enormous sums to building capacity in anticipation of future demand.

The market is increasingly questioning not simply how much AI infrastructure will ultimately be needed, but how quickly it can be delivered, who will finance it and whether the economics will justify the investment.

Under U.S. market-wide circuit-breaker rules, a decline of 7% in the S&P 500 from its previous closing level triggers a 15-minute trading halt if reached before 3:25 p.m. ET. Based on today's thresholds, that level stands at 7,150.41.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

A 13% decline, corresponding to an S&P 500 level of 6,689.09, would trigger another 15-minute halt before 3:25 p.m. A decline of 20%, or a level of 6,150.89, would result in trading being halted for the remainder of the session, regardless of the time.

The rules are based on the S&P 500, rather than the Nasdaq 100 or Dow Jones Industrial Average, and apply across U.S. equity markets.

With the S&P 500 already down 3.8%, traders are monitoring the 7% threshold as the next major line in the sand. However, a Level 1 or Level 2 decline reached at or after 3:25 p.m. ET would not trigger a trading halt, unless the market reaches Level 3.

title: Stock Market Crash Or Rally? Plan For Both

Part of our midterms guide. Start here: what the vote really changes for your money.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

On Monday, the Nasdaq 100 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 peak: a correction, its third this year. On Wednesday, after Democrats won Congress, the Dow rose 3.03% to 53,356, its best day since April 2025, and the S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,689.

Correction on Monday. Rally on Wednesday. Can you predict which one wins next week? Probably not. Nobody can, not reliably. But you can decide now what you'll do either way.

What Does The Data Say?

That this wasn't one market. It was two, moving in opposite directions at the same time. Look at Wednesday alone:

On the Dow's best day since April 2025, power stocks fell 9-14%. "The market" told you nothing about your stocks.

And the AI selloff kept going underneath the rally. In the month to Tuesday, AMD fell 24%, Micron 20%, Alphabet 18% and Dell 27%. On Wednesday, Micron fell another 7%. Meanwhile Centene, Wednesday's winner, was already up 96% over 12 months and just 5% below its 52-week high before the vote.

See more lines: why the two markets moved apart

The vote moved stocks on what a Democratic Congress might do in 2027: health-care money back (insurers and hospitals up), a smaller defense budget (defense down), scrutiny of AI data centers plus a Texas governor who wants to pause new ones (power and data-center builders down). None of those changed a single company's earnings on Wednesday; the new Congress isn't sworn in until January, and President Trump keeps his veto. The AI selloff is older and is about something else: whether roughly $900 billion of AI spending worldwide this year earns its money back. We'll score our own pre-vote calls in a day-after recap.

So Why Does This Feel So Hard?

Because fear and greed arrived on the same day. If you own Vistra, Wednesday felt like a crash. If you own Centene, it felt like a windfall. Both feelings push you to act on the price, right now.

We wrote about this frame in October, when inflation was the fear: Inflation Is Back. Is A Stock Market Crash Next? The point then holds now. Crashes happen: in 2022, the S&P 500 fell 25% from its January high, Nvidia fell 63% and Meta fell 74%. And recoveries happen faster than people expect: after the 1982 low, the S&P 500 rose 58% in a year. Often, the investors who got hurt most weren't the ones who owned the wrong stocks. They were the ones who had to decide what to do in the middle of the move.

Revenue from the company's handset division, its largest business, fell 26% to $5.14 billion, dragging chip segment sales down 8% to $9.02 billion. Qualcomm is facing pressure from rising memory costs, driven by strong data-center demand, as well as slower smartphone sales.

Snap shares tumbled 9.8% in premarket trading to $5.34 after the Snapchat parent reported third-quarter results that fell short of expectations on revenue and user growth.

Revenue came in at $1.72 billion, just below analysts' estimate of $1.73 billion, while daily active users reached 495 million, missing the 499 million expected by Wall Street. Advertising revenue grew just 4% year over year, slowing from 9% growth in the previous quarter.

Dutch Bros shares plunged 13.7% in premarket trading after the coffee chain issued full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance that fell short of analyst expectations, overshadowing a modest third-quarter earnings beat.

The company reported earnings of $0.25 per share, a penny above estimates, while revenue of $549.84 million narrowly topped consensus. However, its full-year 2026 revenue forecast of $2.10 billion came in below the $2.13 billion expected by Wall Street.

EPAM Systems shares surged 13.6% in premarket trading after the digital transformation company reported third-quarter results above analyst expectations and raised its full-year outlook.

Adjusted earnings came in at $3.51 per share, beating the $3.40 consensus, while revenue of $1.426 billion edged past estimates of $1.42 billion and increased 2.3% year over year. The company also raised its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to $13.23 to $13.31 per share and lifted its revenue growth outlook to 3.5% to 3.7%.
